faq.q: Why does my voice sound weird on recordings?
faq.a: When you talk, you hear your voice through the air and through your skull bones, which add deep tones. A recording only picks up the air part, so it sounds higher and thinner than what you are used to.
asks: Why do I hate hearing my voice recorded?
Why does my voice sound different on video?

faq.q: Is my real voice the one on the recording?
faq.a: Yes, the recording is much closer to how other people hear you. Only you hear the extra bone-carried sound.
asks: How do other people hear my voice?

faq.a: Bone conduction is sound travelling through the bones of your skull to your inner ear, without going through the air. Some headphones and hearing aids use it.
asks: How do bone conduction headphones work?
Can you hear through your bones?

faq.q: Why do I sound louder to myself with my ears blocked?
faq.a: Blocking your ears stops sound escaping from the ear canal, so more of the bone-carried sound stays trapped and reaches your inner ear. Your voice sounds boomy and loud.
asks: Why does my voice boom with earplugs in?
Why do I hear my own chewing so loudly?

faq.q: Do singers get used to their recorded voice?
faq.a: Yes. People who often hear recordings of themselves, like singers and presenters, get used to the sound and stop finding it strange.
asks: Will I ever like my recorded voice?
Why do some people like hearing their voice?

facts: You hear your own voice through both air conduction and bone conduction; recordings capture only air-conducted sound.
Bone conduction carries low-pitched sound especially well, making your voice sound deeper to yourself.

quiz.why: When you talk, bone conduction adds deep tones only you hear. The recording, like other people's ears, gets only the air-carried sound.

wrong.0: A normal recording plays back at the same speed you spoke.
wrong.2: Even recordings made without you knowing sound this way.
